idiom_name: template unfold(seed, step, sink) driving a std::function<void(const T&)>
implementation_notes: Pre-coroutine C++ realises the anamorphism by pushing each produced layer into a sink, so nothing has to be materialised and the consumer's callback is the assembly step; termination lives in the step function, which reports whether a next seed exists. Works on any C++11 toolchain and costs one type-erased call per layer, the price of not knowing the concrete consumer type. Compare with the C++23 std::generator sibling, which restores pull semantics and range integration at the cost of a newer toolchain.
pitfalls: The sink must not throw or re-enter the unfold: the scheme holds the state by value and has no unwinding contract.
A recursive C++ unfold grows the stack with structure depth; deep trees need an explicit worklist before C++23.
std::function in the sink adds a type-erasure boundary and a possible allocation per layer - template the sink on hot paths.

variants.name: Stateful generator object with a step cursor (C++17)
variants.idiom_name: class holding the current seed with value()/next(), std::optional<T> as the stop signal
variants.implementation_notes: The pull counterpart without coroutines: an object owns the current state, exposes a valid()/current() pair and advances with a step function, so the consumer drives the unfold one layer at a time and std::optional<T> (C++17) can carry the stop condition in the value type when the step function returns it. This is the shape most pre-C++23 codebases hand-roll when a range interface is required and the toolchain cannot use std::generator.
pitfalls: The object holds live state, so copying it duplicates the generator: iterating the copy does not advance the original - delete or document the copy semantics.
Returning a reference into the object from value() ties the element's lifetime to the generator; return by value unless the elements are large and stable.

variants.name: C++23 std::generator coroutine (co_yield per layer)
variants.idiom_name: std::generator<T> with co_yield, driven by range-for
variants.implementation_notes: C++23 std::generator<T> turns the step function into a coroutine that yields one layer per resume, giving real pull semantics and direct integration with the ranges algorithms (__cpp_lib_generator). Use it when the toolchain is C++23 and consumers prefer ranges to callbacks; the state lives in the coroutine frame instead of in a hand-written object.
pitfalls: The generator owns its coroutine frame: storing it past the iteration or letting it outlive the frame's scope dangles.
Exceptions thrown inside the coroutine surface on the next resume rather than at the call site, which moves error handling to the consumer's loop.
